citations.narrative:
Multiple enclosures are not in good repair with excavated and elevated dig guards, and exposed fasteners sticking out of
surfaces.
In the enclosure housing eleven red foxes, the enclosure housing two African crested porcupines, and the enclosure
housing two mountain lions, the animals have excavated under the wire dig guard.
In the enclosures housing one mountain coati and the enclosure housing one mountain lion and one jaguar, there are
screw/nail heads that the animals can walk upon. In the coati enclosure there is a bench that the wood has degraded
leaving three nail heads exposed without the surrounding wood. In the jaguar/mountain lion enclosure there is a screw
that is exposed where the wood has worn away.
Enclosures that are not kept in good repair can result in injury from entrapment or sharp points. Gaps beneath the wire dig
guards can allow an animal’s foot and leg to pass through and potentially become entrapped or broken. The elevated
screw heads can cause punctures or lacerations to the animal’s feet or skin.
The enclosures must be constructed of such material and of such strength as appropriate for the animals involved. The
housing facilities shall be maintained in good repair to protect the animals from injury and to contain the animals.

The water receptacle for one tiger is not being kept clean and sanitary. In the enclosure housing one tiger, the only
available water source is a round water tank filled with dark green, murky water. USDA inspectors were unable to observe
the sides and bottom of the container.
Water receptacles that are not kept clean and sanitary may contaminate the water, which can have an adverse effect on
the health and well-being of the animals.
All water receptacles shall be kept clean and sanitary.
Correct by June 20, 2026

The facility does not have an effective pest control program in place to control insects. Multiple flies were observed by
USDA inspectors on two red foxes. The tips of the foxes’ ears appeared to have previously healed trauma and areas of
redness on the ear margin. Similar lesions were seen on other red foxes and one male wolf. Flies were attracted to the
tips of the ears, and the foxes flipped their ears to remove the flies. While the pens were kept clean, no other fly control
was seen in the area of the foxes or the wolf (e.g. fly traps or fans).
Pests can pose a hazard to the health and wellbeing of the animals by either irritating or injuring them and exposing them
to potential diseases or illness. A safe and effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and
mammalian pests shall be established and maintained.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
Additional Inspectors:
KATIE PRICE, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
